statement: Nicotine pouches (tobacco-free oral pouches) have been measured in laboratories and surveys far more than in people. Laboratory analyses found nicotine in all the products sold as containing it, in very different amounts, and tobacco-specific nitrosamines absent or in small amounts, well below the amounts reported for snus. An independent German government laboratory (Mallock et al., 2024; intramural funding, no competing interests declared) analysed one pouch of each of 46 products from 20 producers bought online in 2021 (a convenience sample): the 44 that contained nicotine held 1.79 to 47.5 mg per pouch (median 9.48), and the nitrosamine NNN was found in 24 of them (9 below the quantification limit), at most 12.9 ng per pouch; the authors set this beside up to 1,190 ng NNN per pouch of snus and 33 to 323 ng per cigarette in smoke, figures from other studies on other bases. A study designed, interpreted and written by Swedish Match, maker of ZYN pouches and General snus, whose four authors are its employees (Back et al., 2023), found no nitrosamine above its quantification limit (0.01 µg/g, roughly 4 to 8 ng per pouch by the editors' arithmetic) in two ZYN variants, one batch each, against NNN 0.44 and NNK 0.19 µg/g in General snus in the same study, and quantified 4 or 5 of 43 compounds (nicotine included) in ZYN against 19 in snus. A 2026 scoping review (Travis et al., 2026) lists three further analyses: 1.41 to 8.11 mg per pouch in 70 US products, 6.4 against 12.3 mg in tobacco-based pouches in 50, and 2.20 to 56 mg in 31 sold in Germany, with measured nicotine generally at or below the label. In surveys, use is low but rising. In the US, current use among young people in 2024 was 1.8 in 100 (National Youth Tobacco Survey, middle and high school; 0.8 in 100 in 2021) and 2.6 in 100 (Monitoring the Future, grades 10 and 12; 1.3 in 100 in 2023; most also vaped), but 0.2 in 100 among 12- to 17-year-olds in the PATH study in 2022–23; among adults in 2022–23 it was 0.4 to 0.8 in 100; elsewhere current use ranged from 0.4 in 100 (adults in England, 2023) to 19 in 100 (youth and adults in Australia, 2023), from surveys of different kinds. Use was more likely in males, younger people and people who currently or formerly smoked, vaped or used smokeless tobacco; US sales rose from 327 to 1,046 million units between July 2021 and May 2024. In people, pouches have been followed for 6 months at most. A 2026 systematic review without meta-analysis (Kopa-Stojak, 2026; critically low confidence by the editors) found 15 pouch studies, none following disease or death. In a non-industry-funded German crossover study of adults who smoked daily (as described by the scoping review), a 30 mg pouch gave more nicotine than a cigarette and 20 mg and 6 mg pouches less, and the 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic blood pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette; industry-funded series found 4 mg and 8 mg pouches below a cigarette and, in people who used snus, pouches giving more nicotine than snus, and nicotine peaked later with pouches (20 to 42 minutes) than with a cigarette (5 to 7). In a small US survey sample, nicotine breakdown products in people who used only pouches were comparable to those in people who smoked, with lower cadmium and uranium; in a 4-week trial, nitrosamine levels were not lowered in people who cut their cigarettes with pouches. Oral findings were compared in small studies: oral lesions in 79 in 100 young Swedish adults who used pouches against 89 in 100 who used snus (a cross-sectional comparison of 126 and 63 people), and less gum inflammation after 24 weeks in an Altria-funded trial of adults who switched from smoking to pouches than in those who kept smoking. The scoping review's authors say the health effects remain largely understudied, that evidence of short-term benefit from switching is limited and mainly industry-funded, and that pouches may be a less hazardous alternative to traditional tobacco but are not risk-free. No source read follows heart disease, cancer, lung disease or death in people who use pouches, or compares them with people who use no nicotine on any health outcome; the product analyses read come from Germany, the United States and a few other countries, and the independent one bought its products in 2021. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (the contents and survey findings).
plain: Nicotine pouches have been measured in laboratories and surveys far more than in people. A German government laboratory tested 46 pouch products and found nicotine in widely different amounts and small amounts of one family of cancer-linked chemicals (nitrosamines) in 26 of the 44 that held nicotine, far below the amounts reported for snus; a test paid for by the maker of ZYN found none above the lowest amount it could measure in its own pouches. In US surveys in 2024, between 1.8 and 2.6 in 100 school-age young people said they currently used pouches (in one survey most also vaped), and fewer than 1 in 100 adults did in 2022–23. In people, pouches have been followed for 6 months at most and no study read has followed illness or death, so nobody yet knows how they compare with snus, with smoking or with using no nicotine for health. Small studies show that pouches deliver nicotine more slowly than a cigarette, in amounts that vary with the pouch, from less to more than a cigarette. The authors of the latest review say pouches may be less hazardous than traditional tobacco but are not risk-free.
population: Tobacco-free nicotine pouches on sale in Germany (46 products bought online in 2021), the United States and other countries; people who use them in national surveys (US youth and adults 2021 to 2024, other countries), crossover studies of 30 to 42 adults and small trials of 30 to 100 adults; a 2026 scoping review of 135 studies to September 2025
exposure: Nicotine pouches: measured product contents; use as reported in surveys; short-term effects in single sessions up to 6 months of follow-up
comparator: Snus; cigarettes; nicotine gum and lozenges; people who use no nicotine (the last not compared on any health outcome in the sources read)
outcome: Measured nicotine, nitrosamine and other constituents; how many people use pouches and who they are; short-term nicotine uptake, blood pressure, arterial stiffness and biomarkers; health outcomes in people (none beyond 6 months, none for disease or death)
magnitude: Mallock et al. 2024 (46 products, 20 producers, bought online January–May 2021; 44 with nicotine, 2 nicotine-free): nicotine 1.79–47.5 mg per pouch, median 9.48 (interquartile range 5.50–16.6), two above 40 mg; median extract pH 8.8 (range 5.5–10.5); printed milligram content on 15 of 44, a score or word on 38, none on 4; tobacco-specific nitrosamines found in 26 of 44: NNN in 24 (9 below the quantification limit of about 0.4 ng), NNK in 3, NAT in 6, NAB in 5; highest per pouch NNN 12.9 ng, NNK 5.4, NAT 2.7, NAB 5.6 (one pouch per product, single analysis); for comparison the authors cite up to 1,190 ng NNN and 120 ng NNK per pouch of snus, 2 ng NNN per gram of nicotine gum and 33–323 ng NNN and 40–246 ng NNK per cigarette in smoke (other studies, other bases). Back et al. 2023 (Swedish Match; 7 products, one batch each): nitrosamines none of ten above quantification limits (0.01 µg/g for NNN, NNK, NAT, NAB) in two ZYN variants and two nicotine replacement products; General snus NNN 0.44, NNK 0.19 µg/g; moist snuff NNN 3.63 and 2.53, NNK 2.27 and 0.92; compounds quantified (nicotine included) of 43: lozenge 2, ZYN moist 4, ZYN dry 5, gum 9, snus 19, moist snuff 26 and 27; ZYN dry and moist formaldehyde 10.3 and 1.5, chromium 0.160 and 0.099, ammonia 62 and 66 µg/g, nickel 0.067 in the dry variant only; total nicotine mg/g ZYN dry 7.63, ZYN moist 12.00, snus 8.13, lozenge 3.20, gum 1.30. Travis et al. 2026 as described (135 studies to September 2025; no risk-of-bias assessment): US 70 tobacco-free products 1.41–8.11 mg per pouch; 50 pouches 6.4 (SD 3.5) against 12.3 (SD 8.2) mg in tobacco-based pouches, free-base share 63.4% against 47.2%; 31 pouches in Germany 2.20–56 mg. US youth current use: National Youth Tobacco Survey (middle and high school) 0.8% (2021) to 1.8% (2024), lifetime 1.9% to 3.5%; Monitoring the Future (grades 10 and 12) 1.3% (2023) to 2.6% (2024), lifetime 3% to 5.4%; PATH ages 12–17 (2022–23) lifetime 0.9%, current 0.2%; of adolescents currently using in 2024, 29% frequent and 22% daily. US adults 2022–23: PATH lifetime 3.3%, current 0.8%; TUS-CPS 2.7% and 0.4%. Other countries, lifetime (current): British youth 2024 3.3% (1.2%); Quebec adolescents 3.7% (2.6%); Australia 2023 26% (19%); Finland 2022 14.4% (3.7%); Poland adults 2024 9.2% (4.3%); Canadian college students 2024 27% (12%); England adults 2023 current 0.4%. Nicotine uptake: independent German crossover 30 mg > cigarette > 20 mg > 6 mg (peak and total over 4 hours; time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); industry series 4 mg and 8 mg below a cigarette, 12 mg and 8 mg mini comparable or higher, time to peak 35–40 minutes against 5–7; in adults using snus, 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches gave higher peak and 60-minute nicotine than 11.2 mg snus. 20 mg and 30 mg pouches raised systolic pressure and arterial stiffness comparably to a cigarette. Sales 327 million units (July 2021) to 1,046 million (May 2024). Kopa-Stojak 2026: 15 pouch studies, longest follow-up 6 months, none on disease or death; crossover trials of 30–42 adults; a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start) quitting odds 1.29 (1.04–1.59) for fruit-flavoured and 1.04 (0.82–1.28) for mint-flavoured pouches; Saudi surveys without comparison groups (for example bloating 66.7%, difficulty breathing 40.5%).

evidence.extracted: Pouch heart and blood pressure effects: in a single-use crossover study of 30 people who use snus or pouches, changes measured 30 minutes after use were, by strength, systolic pressure -1% (6 mg), +3% (9 mg) and +1.4% (11.2 mg), diastolic +4.5%, +7.4% and +3.9%, and heart rate -3%, +3.2% and -0.2%; in a survey with no comparison group 28.4% of people who use pouches reported rapid or irregular heartbeat. The text calls the 11.2 mg product snus and gives its heart-rate change as +0.2%; Table 6 labels it a pouch and gives -0.2%.

evidence.locator: Table 6; Results › Pouches › Gastrointestinal Health, Respiratory System, Oral Health and Mental Health, 1st paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Pouch symptoms in Saudi Arabian surveys without comparison groups: bloating 66.7%, nausea 47.9%, heartburn 46.7%, difficulty breathing 40.5%, frequent cough or wheeze 27.8%, any psychological effect 39.3%, taste or smell change 36.7%, dry mouth 39.8%. These are prevalences in people who use pouches only; no estimate of what share of a comparable group without pouches would report the same symptoms.

evidence.locator: Results › Pouches › Oral Health, 1st paragraph; Table 6
evidence.extracted: Pouch oral findings: among 272 young Swedish adults, oral lesions 79% and hyperkeratosis 65% in people who use pouches (n = 126) against 89% and 79% in people who use snus (n = 63); erythema 44% and mucosal ulcers 2% in the pouch group; gingival recession 45% against 52%. After 23 dentists switched from snus to pouches, snus lesion severity fell from 95.7% to 69.6% and gingival irritation from 43.5% to 4.3%. In a randomized trial of adults who smoked (n printed as 155), gingival and bleeding indices were 20% to 30% lower at 12 and 24 weeks after switching to pouches than with continued smoking (the Altria-funded trial named in the scoping review).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Authors' stated limitations: many studies of men only; few data on pouches; self-reported use; no meta-analysis because of heterogeneity; most studies from Scandinavia and Swedish snus differs from products elsewhere; observational designs prevent establishing causality; brands, nicotine content and flavours vary; quality not always satisfactory. Conclusion: too little data to clearly determine the health effects of pouches.

risk_of_bias.note: The product analyses are samples of convenience or chosen by a maker (46 products bought online in Germany in 2021; 7 products, 2 pouch variants, picked and supplied by the funder), one pouch per product in a single analysis, with nitrosamine results of at most 12.9 ng per pouch and many below the quantification limit (cards sc_mallock_2024 and sc_back_2023, overall high on the worst-domain rule). The scoping review made no risk-of-bias assessment (AMSTAR 2 critically low), and the systematic review is critically low confidence. Industry funding is reported as printed and the findings are set beside independent ones, not dropped.

inconsistency.note: The figures differ for known reasons (different products, markets, populations and quantification limits) and agree in direction: nitrosamines low or absent in both the independent and the maker's analyses, nicotine content varying widely, use low and rising. The uptake studies differ with strength, as expected.

indirectness.note: Product content is not health; the human measures are short sessions or weeks and mostly seen through two reviews; the products were bought in 2021 to 2025 in a few countries; the independent analysis compares with snus and cigarettes using other studies' figures on other bases; no source read compares pouches with using no nicotine on any health outcome.

imprecision.note: Wide ranges (nicotine 1.41 to 56 mg per pouch across studies) show variation between products, not imprecision of an estimate; surveys are large; trial effects are not part of this claim.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources. 12 of the 73 new studies in the scoping review are industry-funded and are set beside the others; the maker's analysis and the independent one agree in direction.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claim; not upgraded for large effect (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Nicotine uptake rose with pouch strength in the crossover studies, but that is a pharmacokinetic finding, not a health effect; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Not applicable to a description of contents and prevalence.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive evidence starts low like other observational evidence and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. The claim is worded as a description of measurements (contents, prevalence, short-term measures) and of what has not been measured (disease or death, anything beyond 6 months), not as an effect of pouches on health, so it is rated as worded and not upgraded for a large effect. Status replicated applies to the contents and survey findings, shown by independent laboratories and surveys that agree in direction (the independent German laboratory, the maker's laboratory and the analyses described by the scoping review; US national surveys); it does not apply to health effects, for which there is no evidence beyond short studies. Overlapping reports are counted once: the systematic review and the scoping review share some primary studies (for example two crossover trials and the oral-health trial), the systematic review cites both laboratory papers read here and the scoping review cites neither.

(PMC author manuscript; Figure 1 and supplement not read) and Kopa-Stojak (Springer HTML, Tables 1 to 6; Online Resources not read). Funders and interests as printed are in the anchors: Mallock et al. is funded by the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment with no competing interests; Back et al. is funded, designed, interpreted and written by Swedish Match, whose four authors are its employees (its quantification limit is roughly ten times or more above the independent laboratory's, so the two sets of results are not directly comparable); Travis et al. is funded by US NIH/NCI/FDA with conflicts printed for two authors and twelve of its 73 new studies are industry-funded; Kopa-Stojak is funded by its university. The primary studies behind the scoping review's content, uptake and prevalence figures are known only through that review (Tran 2024, Page 2025, Reimann 2024 and others have no reference record here). Whether pouches help people stop smoking is a separate claim. Section 7 is the senior author's: this is a draft for decision p-ways-of-taking.
